claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical lamellar microstructure containing fine dual-phase colonies.
The untreated alloy has high strength at room temperature.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
Boundary-localized stress concentrations and microcracking cause the limited tensile ductility of the untreated alloy.
The untreated alloy has less than 10% room-temperature tensile elongation.
Brittle interphase fracture is responsible for the untreated alloy's limited tensile elongation.
Adding 0.1–0.5 atomic percent boron will promote boron segregation at interphase boundaries.
Boron segregation will strengthen the interphase boundaries.
Boundary-localized boron will improve interface cohesion.
Boundary-localized boron will reduce delamination between the joined phases.
Boron modifies local bonding at the interphase boundaries.
Boron-strengthened boundaries will reduce dislocation pile-ups or prevent them from producing critical local stress concentrations.
Reducing pile-up-induced stress concentrations will mitigate microcrack initiation at hard/soft lamellar interfaces.
The boron-modified alloy will have yield and tensile strengths within ±10% of those of the untreated alloy.
The boron-modified alloy will have at least 50% greater elongation to failure than the untreated alloy.
The intervention is most effective when interphase-boundary cohesion is the dominant factor controlling crack initiation in a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
Excessive boron can form coarse borides and increase brittleness.
The optimal boron concentration depends on alloy composition and processing details.
